plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic array of circles arranged in six vertical columns, with arrows drawn among them and part of the field sitting on a gray background. Five columns hold five circles each, evenly stacked from top to bottom, while the rightmost column holds only three. In every full column the circle in the middle position is an open white disk and the remaining circles are filled solid black. The white disk in the third column from the left carries the italic label x. Straight vertical arrows within each full column run upward from lower circles to the middle disk and from that disk to the circle above, and long curved arrows arc from a column's bottom circle to its topmost one. Along the row of white disks, horizontal arrows point inward toward x: the disks in the fourth through sixth columns send arrows leftward into x, with farther ones curving above intervening columns, and x in turn sends arrows leftward to the disks in the second and first columns. A rounded gray region with stepped edges covers the two circles below x in its own column together with the white disk and every circle beneath it in each column to the right. Because each arrow encodes an ordering between two elements, the shaded block gathers the elements the arrow chains place on one side of x, turning a counting argument about the quality of a partition into a visible area.

elements: six vertical columns of circles; columns 1-5 hold 5 circles each, column 6 holds 3 (bottom, middle, top aligned with the others' bottom/middle/top rows)
open white disk at the middle (3rd) position of each full column; all other circles filled black
italic label 'x' beside the white disk in column 3 (the median-of-medians)

straight vertical arrows in each full column: bottom→2nd→white disk, white disk→4th→top (all pointing toward/away from the white disk as in source: upward into the white disk from below, upward out of it above)
curved arc arrow in each full column from the bottom circle up to the topmost circle (left-bowing arcs)

horizontal straight arrows between adjacent white disks along the middle row, pointing left: disk6→disk5 (none, disk6 curves), disk5→disk4... x receives arrows from columns 4 and 5; x sends arrows leftward to columns 2 and 1
long curved arrows from the white disks of columns 5 and 6 arcing above intervening columns into x / into the leftward chain

rounded gray stepped region covering: the two circles below x in column 3 (including x's column rows 1-2, but not x itself), and the white disk plus both circles below it in columns 4 and 5, and column 6's middle and bottom circles
arrowheads on every arrow (filled triangular heads)

interactions.label: Proof step
interactions.teaches: Builds SELECT's counting argument one layer at a time: first the array is grouped into columns of five, then each column's median is marked (white disks), then the median-of-medians x is chosen, and only then are the elements provably greater than x shaded — the learner sees that the shaded count follows from the arrow chains, not from direct comparisons

Clicking x brightens exactly the arrow chains and circles that transitively certify 'greater than x' (each column's upper half via vertical arrows, then right-column medians via the horizontal arrows into x), showing why 3 elements per right-hand column can be counted without comparing each one to x directly

interactions.label: Certified side
interactions.teaches: Mirrors the shaded region to the symmetric block of elements provably less than x (left columns' lower halves via reversed arrow chains), making the two-sided partition guarantee — at least ~3n/10 on each side — visible

demo_steps.title: Group into fives
demo_steps.narration: The array is drawn as columns of five elements (the last column is short). No ordering is known yet — just the grouping.

demo_steps.title: Mark each column's median
demo_steps.narration: The middle circle of each column turns white: it is that column's median, with two elements below and two above it (vertical arrows certify the order).

demo_steps.title: Choose x, the median of medians
demo_steps.narration: x is selected among the white disks. Horizontal arrows between medians appear: medians to x's right are ≥ x, and x is ≥ the medians to its left.

demo_steps.title: Shade the certified region
demo_steps.narration: The gray block appears: in each column whose median is ≥ x, the median and the two elements above it (here drawn as the block to the lower/right per the source layout) are known to be on one side of x — at least 3 elements from each of half the columns, without any direct comparison to x.

demo_steps.title: The symmetric argument
demo_steps.narration: Flip the toggle: the mirror-image block on the other side of x is shaded, showing the same counting argument guarantees elements less than x as well.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Flat 2D diagram on a white page. Six columns at world x = 0,1.6,3.2,4.8,6.4,8.0; five rows at y = 0,1.5,3.0,4.5,6.0. Columns 1-5 have all five rows; column 6 has only rows y=0,3.0,6.0 (bottom, middle, top — note middle at y=3.0 and top at y=6.0, skipping the intermediate rows as drawn). Circles: radius ~0.32; black fill #111 for ordinary elements, white fill #ffffff with black stroke for column medians (row y=3.0 of columns 1-5, and column 6's y=3.0 circle is also white per source — it participates in the median row). Label 'x' in italic serif just right of column 3's white disk. Vertical straight arrows along each full column connecting consecutive circles (drawn in the gaps, with arrowheads). Curved arcs bowing ~0.5 units left of each column from the bottom circle (y=0) to the top (y=6.0). Horizontal arrows between adjacent white disks at y=3.0 pointing left (col5→col4→x, x→col2→col1), plus two long shallow arcs above the row: from col5's and col6's white disks curving up ~1 unit and landing on x (col6→x arcs over col5). Gray region: rounded-rect (#b8b8b8, ~0.55 opacity) with a stepped top edge, covering column 3 rows y=0..1.5, columns 4-5 rows y=0..3.0 (including their white disks), and column 6 rows y=0..3.0 — i.e. the 'known greater' block per CLRS convention where arrows point from larger to smaller; keep the exact source coverage. In the 'Less than x' toggle, shade the mirror block: column 1 rows y=4.5..6.0... concretely columns 1-2 rows above their medians plus x's column rows y=4.5..6.0.
interactionPlan.notes: Render as a pure 2D scene (orthographic camera, flat planes/circles via CircleGeometry and quadratic-curve TubeGeometry or fat lines for arrows; arrowheads as small cones laid flat). Proof phases show/hide prebuilt layers: phase 'grouped' = circles only; 'medians' = white median disks + vertical arrows; 'xChosen' = label x + horizontal/curved median arrows; 'shaded' = gray region. Click on x (raycast the disk) toggles an emissive/bright highlight (#ff8800 or scale-up stroke) on the certifying chains: for 'Greater' that is the upper-half vertical arrows and top circles of columns 4-6 plus the horizontal arrows into x; for 'Less', the mirror chains through columns 1-2. Keep both gray regions prebuilt and crossfade on toggle.

authoredContext: We now examine a selection algorithm whose running time is O.n/ in the worst case. Like RANDOMIZED-SELECT, the algorithm SELECT finds the desired element by recursively partitioning the input array. Here, however, we guarantee a good split upon partitioning the array. SELECT uses the deterministic partitioning algorithm PARTITION from quicksort (see Section 7.1), but modified to take the element to partition around as an input parameter. The SELECT algorithm determines the ith smallest of an input array of n > 1 distinct elements by executing the following steps. (If n D 1, then SELECT merely returns its only input value as the ith smallest.) 1. Divide the n elements of the input array into bn=5c groups of 5 elements each and at most one group made up of the remaining n mod 5 elements. 2. Find the median of each of the dn=5e groups by first insertion-sorting the elements of each group (of which there are at most 5) and then picking the median from the sorted list of group elements. 3. Use SELECT recursively to find the median x of the dn=5e medians found in step 2. (If there are an even number of medians, then by our convention, x is the lower median.) 4. Partition the input array around the median-of-medians x using the modified version of PARTITION. Let k be one more than the number of elements on the low side of the partition, so that x is the kth smallest element and there are nk elements on the high side of the partition. 5. If i D k, then return x. Otherwise, use SELECT recursively to find the ith smallest element on the low side if i < k, or the .i k/th smallest element on the high side if i > k. To analyze the running time of SELECT, we first determine a lower bound on the number of elements that are greater than the partitioning element x. Figure 9.1 helps us to visualize this bookkeeping.

discrepancies: Default view (phase 1) shows only bare black circles with no arrows, white median disks, or shading — the figure is unrecognizable until the user clicks through the proof-step buttons, whereas the source shows the fully annotated diagram

The long curved column arrows in the source sweep along the left side of each column (bottom-to-top, visibly bowed); in the generated figure the single per-column arc is subtler and partially overlaps the straight vertical arrows

The gray shaded region's stepped boundary is approximate — in the source it hugs the white median row and right columns with a distinctive notch around x, while the generated shape is a generic two-step block
The 'Less than x' mirror shading is an addition not present in the source figure (source shades only one side)
evaluation.notes: All core elements of the median-of-medians diagram (column groups, white median row, certifying arrow chains into x, stepped gray region) are faithfully built with strong step-through pedagogy; the main weakness is that the default state hides nearly everything behind the phase buttons, and the gray region shape is only approximate.
action_items: Make the default view the fully-shaded final state (matching the source figure) so the figure is recognizable immediately, with the phase buttons rewinding it
Refine the gray region outline to match the source's stepped contour with the notch hugging the median row near x
Emphasize the long bowed column arcs (greater curvature, slight left offset) so they read as clearly as in the source
